preamble: Pharyngealization (emphaticization) of plain [t] to the emphatic [tˤ], Arabic ṭāʾ ط. The documented cases are loanwords in Arabic, in which a European t is taken over as ṭ: Spanish tomate > طماطم ṭamāṭim, French pantalon > بنطلون banṭalōn. In these words every t of the source becomes emphatic, and the narrow transcriptions show backed vowels, as in Egyptian [tˤɑˈmɑːtˤɪm]. Ottoman Turkish پاتاتس patates, written with plain ت, likewise gives Egyptian and Hijazi baṭāṭis /ba.tˤaː.tˤis/ (Wiktionary also lists a variant بَتَاتَا with plain t), and Greek τραπέζι trapézi gives Sudanese Arabic ṭarabēza 'table' (Wikipedia, Juba Arabic). Ge'ez and Amharic often treat Greek t in a parallel way, as the ejective ṭ [tʼ] (filed under [t] > [tʼ]). The reverse change, loss of emphasis in Maltese, Cypriot Arabic and Israeli Hebrew, is filed under [tˤ] > [t].

examples.note: Both t become ṭ; Wiktionary says the word was reshaped as a plural pattern. Hijazi has the same /tˤa.maː.tˤim/.
South Levantine baṭāṭa [bɑˈtˤɑː.tˤɑ] 'potatoes' and Moroccan baṭāṭa continue the Arabic form (Wiktionary).
Hijazi and South Levantine have the same banṭalōn.

examples.to: Egyptian طنط ṭanṭ [tˤɑntˤ], a respectful term to address an older woman
